title: Gini coefficient of scientists and universities
authors: Klaus M. Frahm, Dima L. Shepelyansky
abstract: Using the public database of Google Scholar article citations of scientists and universities we apply the algorithm for constructing Lorenz curves to the resulting citation distributions. Using Lorenz and Pareto curves, broadly used for economic analyses of wealth inequality across countries, we show that this approach gives a useful insight of citation distributions of world-leading scientists characterized by the Gini coefficient $G$ obtained from the Lorenz curves. For articles of 15 Nobel laureates (including A. Einstein and R. Feynman) we find the average $G=0.81$ with 50% of articles capturing only 2.7% of all citations and the top 10% (1%) of articles capturing 71% (30%) of all citations. Furthmore, we determine for world-leading universities the Gini coefficient via the citations of affiliated scientists. We show that about 65 percent of all citations belonging to a university (e.g. Princeton, Cambridge) are generated only by 10 percent of their university scientists while 50% of scientists produce only 3% of all university citations. The citation distributions are well described by the concept of Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation with similarities traced to the world wealth inequality.
summary: This paper analyzes the inequality in scientific recognition by applying economic measures like the Gini coefficient to citation data. It models these citation distributions using advanced concepts from statistical mechanics, specifically the Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization framework. The findings demonstrate that citation accumulation follows highly unequal patterns, mirroring global wealth distribution.
main_problem: The paper applies concepts from economic inequality, specifically the Gini coefficient, to analyze the citation distributions of scientists and universities.
main_result: The citation distributions exhibit high levels of inequality (e.g., average Gini coefficient of 0.81 for Nobel laureates), which can be modeled using concepts from statistical mechanics like Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization.
method: The authors construct Lorenz and Pareto curves using citation counts as proxies for wealth, and then fit these empirical curves to theoretical models derived from statistical mechanics.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the citation network of scientists and universities. The theoretical framework employs the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH) and models the distribution using Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) and extended RJ (RJE) statistical distributions.
key_observables: Gini coefficient (G), Lorenz curve, Pareto curve, and citation shares held by the top percentiles of scientists/universities.
important_parameters: Gini coefficient (G), temperature/chemical potential parameters ($\epsilon, a, \mu$), and citation thresholds ($N_{min}=500$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is the analogy between citation counts and economic wealth ($c_m = w_m$), and that the underlying distribution follows a thermalized state described by RJ statistics.
figures_summary: Figures compare the empirical Lorenz and Pareto curves for various datasets (e.g., Princeton, World 2021, Nobel laureates) against theoretical curves derived from RJE and RJS models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the data sets, introducing the Rayleigh-Jeans properties, detailing the curve construction methods, presenting the main results (including specific Gini values), and discussing the thermalization assumptions.
why_interesting: While the subject matter is bibliometrics, the rigorous application of statistical mechanics concepts (RJ/RJE distributions, thermalization) to model complex, emergent distributions of scientific recognition provides a powerful analogy for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

The x-axis corresponds to the cumulative fraction of households/papers (h) and the y-axis to the cumulative fraction of wealth/citations (w). The dashed black line corresponds to the line of perfect equipartition w = h. The corresponding values of a and ε have been determined by minimizing the geometrical curve distance between both curves and such that they have the same Gini coefficient G = 0.883.
